label: Separation in the Plane
notes: Open the chapter, which spans printed pages 372 through 402. We apply the fundamental group to the geometry of the plane. The central result is the Jordan curve theorem, that a simple closed curve separates the plane into two regions, and its powerful relatives, the separation theorem, invariance of domain, and the winding number.

label: The Jordan Curve Theorem
notes: The Jordan curve theorem states that a simple closed curve in the plane divides it into exactly two connected components, a bounded inside and an unbounded outside, and is their common boundary. Intuitively obvious yet famously hard to prove, it is established here using the fundamental group and covering space machinery.

label: The Jordan Separation Theorem
notes: A preliminary separation theorem shows that any arc in the plane does not separate it, while a simple closed curve separates it into at least two pieces. These local-to-global statements are assembled with Mayer-Vietoris style arguments on fundamental groups to control how subsets disconnect the plane. They build directly toward the full Jordan theorem.

label: Invariance of Domain
notes: Invariance of domain asserts that a continuous injective map from an open subset of the plane into the plane is open, so its image is open and the map is a homeomorphism onto it. This guarantees dimension is a topological invariant in low dimensions and forbids the plane from embedding into a line.

label: The Winding Number
notes: The winding number of a loop about a point counts net signed revolutions and is computed from the fundamental group of the punctured plane. It is invariant under homotopies avoiding the point and provides the quantitative tool that distinguishes inside from outside in the Jordan curve theorem and detects when curves enclose a region.

label: Imbeddings of Graphs
notes: The chapter closes with which graphs imbed in the plane. The nonplanarity of the complete graph on five vertices and the utility graph follows from separation arguments, anticipating Kuratowski's theorem. These results show the fundamental group governing concrete combinatorial geometry. Next: the Seifert-van Kampen theorem.
